title: From Light-Sensitive Cells to Vertebrate Eyes
subtitle: Trace how light detection, pigment, lenses, layered retinas, and color vision accumulated along the chordate branch.
introduction: Living species are not frozen ancestors. Each stop is a surviving cousin that preserves evidence about traits inferred for successive branches of chordate history. The map shows their real relationships; dates describe divergences or fossil evidence, not the age of the living species.

completion.title: Light became a detailed world
completion.summary: You followed evidence from a few light-sensitive cells to the focusing optics, layered retina, and specialized color vision of living vertebrates.

steps.title: A direction for light
steps.summary: Lancelets possess small frontal photoreceptive organs rather than a vertebrate camera eye. Pigment beside light-sensitive cells helps distinguish the direction of illumination, turning simple detection into spatial information.
steps.evidence: Developmental genes and ciliary photoreceptors in lancelets share parts of the molecular toolkit later used to construct vertebrate eyes and retinas.
steps.uncertainty: Modern lancelets are specialized living cousins, so their organs are comparisons rather than direct replicas of an ancestral chordate eye.

image.alt: A translucent European lancelet showing its narrow fish-like chordate body
image.caption: A living lancelet preserves a chordate body plan with small frontal photoreceptive organs.

sources.label: Lamb et al., Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2007)

steps.title: An ocellus guides a larva
steps.summary: A sea-squirt larva carries an ocellus containing photoreceptors and a pigment cell. It cannot form a detailed image, but it can steer the swimming larva by reporting light direction and intensity.
steps.evidence: The larval ocellus combines ciliary photoreceptors, pigment, and neural connections, providing a comparative model for an early chordate light-sensing circuit.
steps.uncertainty: Tunicates are the closest living invertebrate relatives of vertebrates, but their compact larval sensory system has its own long evolutionary history.

image.alt: A translucent sea squirt attached to a rock beneath the water
image.caption: Adult sea squirts look simple, while their mobile larvae carry a directional light-sensing ocellus.

sources.label: Lamb, Progress in Retinal and Eye Research (2022)

steps.title: A vertebrate eye in reduced light
steps.summary: The Pacific hagfish has small eyes beneath translucent skin. Its retina and photoreceptors retain vertebrate features, yet its dim habitat and life history are associated with greatly reduced image-forming structures.
steps.evidence: Comparisons of hagfish development, retinal organization, and genes help separate ancient vertebrate features from reductions that evolved within hagfish.
steps.uncertainty: A simple-looking living eye is not automatically ancestral; researchers debate how much hagfish anatomy reflects secondary reduction.

image.alt: A Pacific hagfish with an elongated body and small head
image.caption: The Pacific hagfish offers evidence from a living jawless vertebrate with strongly reduced eyes.

sources.label: Oisi et al., Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology (2022)

steps.title: The camera eye is assembled
steps.summary: Adult lampreys possess a cornea, lens, iris, layered retina, rods, and cones. The basic vertebrate camera-eye architecture was therefore established before jawless and jawed vertebrates separated.
steps.evidence: Lamprey retinal cell types and gene-expression programs reveal deep homology with the conserved retina of jawed vertebrates, despite later lineage-specific changes.
steps.uncertainty: Lampreys are modern animals, and their complex eyes do not show one historical moment; ancestral states are inferred through comparison and fossils.

image.alt: A sea lamprey viewed from the side with its eye visible
image.caption: The sea lamprey has the main optical and retinal components of a vertebrate camera eye.

steps.title: Color channels multiply
steps.summary: Zebrafish use four cone classes sensitive to ultraviolet, short, medium, and long wavelengths. Duplicated opsin genes and patterned cone mosaics expanded what a vertebrate retina could distinguish.
steps.evidence: Genetics, physiology, and retinal imaging connect specific zebrafish opsins and cone types with wavelength-sensitive visual circuits.
steps.uncertainty: Four-channel zebrafish vision is one specialized outcome of fish evolution, not a universal stage through which every vertebrate passed.

image.alt: A striped zebrafish swimming against a plain background
image.caption: Zebrafish retinas organize several cone types into a highly patterned color-sensing mosaic.

sources.label: Baden and Osorio, Annual Review of Vision Science (2019)

steps.title: Eyes move onto land
steps.summary: Frogs inherit the vertebrate camera eye but must operate across water, air, and metamorphosis. Changes to focusing, eyelids, tear films, and visual circuits accompanied the move into terrestrial environments.
steps.evidence: Amphibian development shows the conserved vertebrate eye program repeatedly adapting as a larva becomes a terrestrial or semi-aquatic adult.
steps.uncertainty: The African clawed frog is secondarily aquatic, so it illustrates developmental conservation and adaptation rather than the first land-going eye.

image.alt: An African clawed frog showing its upward-facing eyes
image.caption: The African clawed frog retains a tetrapod eye while living a secondarily aquatic life.

steps.title: A retina tuned to darkness
steps.summary: Mouse retinas are dominated by highly sensitive rods, reflecting the nocturnal history of early mammals. Neural pooling sacrifices fine detail while improving the detection of scarce photons.
steps.evidence: Mammalian retinal anatomy, opsins, and visual behavior document a deep low-light specialization followed by later reinvention of color and acuity in some branches.
steps.uncertainty: Mice are an extreme modern nocturnal example; early mammal vision varied, and soft retinal tissues rarely fossilize directly.

image.alt: A small house mouse photographed in side view
image.caption: The house mouse represents a mammalian retina strongly weighted toward sensitive low-light vision.

steps.title: High-acuity primate sight
steps.summary: Human vision concentrates cones in a tiny fovea for detailed central sight and uses three cone pigments for trichromatic color. Eye movements rapidly place important features onto that high-resolution region.
steps.evidence: Anatomy, genetics, and psychophysics connect primate foveal organization and duplicated cone opsins with fine spatial discrimination and red–green color vision.
steps.uncertainty: Human sight is one specialized primate solution, with narrow spectral reach and a blind spot; it is not a measure of evolutionary progress.

image.alt: Close-up photograph of a human iris and pupil
image.caption: A human eye feeds a fovea-centered, trichromatic visual system inherited from primate ancestors.

sources.label: Jacobs, Evolution of colour vision in mammals (2009)
